newsitem.title: USA: Rights group condemns Bahrain's "shameful policies".
newsitem.headline: Rights group condemns Bahrain's "shameful policies".

text.p: Widescale government and security force violations of civil and political rights in Bahrain are a major factor behind unrest in the Gulf Arab state, Human Rights Watch said on Wednesday.

The privately funded non-government group, in a report on the tiny island which is the headquarters of the U.S. Fifth Fleet, criticised U.S. government refusal to speak out publicly about abusive practices in Bahrain.
"Washington's silence in the face of flagrant human rights violations by its Persian Gulf allies is inevitably read as tacit acceptance," said Kenneth Roth, HRW executive director.

"The absence of any public reproach to Bahrain for its shameful policies stands in disappointing contrast to the Clinton administration's lofty pronouncements about human rights and democracy in general," he said.
Bahrain, the Gulf's banking and financial centre, has been the scene since December 1994 of unrest that has flared sporadically into violence including bombings, arson and riots.

Members of the island's majority Shi'ite Moslem community seek economic and political reforms from their Sunni Moslem rulers. More than 30 people have been killed in the unrest and hundreds of protesters and religious leaders have been arrested.
The government has accused Shi'ite Iran of stirring up trouble -- a charge denied by Tehran and discredited by HRW.
The 109-page report, based on interviews with Bahraini residents including lawyers and business leaders and people forcibly exiled by the government, said it found two basic categories of violations.

"The first, relating to law enforcement and administration of justice, includes arbitrary detention, physical abuse of detainees, and special security courts that deny elementary due process rights," said Joe Stork, advocacy director of Human Rights Watch/Middle East.

"The second category covers basic political rights such as the freedom to speak out and to hold meetings, form political parties and criticise government policies. Bahrainis risk arrest and physical abuse, and even exile, for demanding that the government abide by the 1973 constitution."

HRW said such abuses as torture were common and went unpunished. Uncorroborated confessions secured in the absence of lawyers were sufficient for security court convictions which could not be appealed. Arbitrary detention and forced exile were practiced as matters of state policy.

"Human Rights Watch concludes that the contention of the government of Bahrain, that the unrest of the past two and a half years can be wholly ascribed to Iranian-sponsored 'terrorism,' lacks credibility," it said.

The group strongly urged the United States and Britain to use their close and longstanding military and political ties with Bahrain to press the ruling al-Khalifa family publicly to end abusive practices which were recurrent, systematic, and matters of state policy, and to make clear that persistent human rights violations would affect negatively the depth and quality of overall relations, including military and security ties.
